<reason>Both sides argued the motion as written and clashed cleanly on the decisive clause ("no reduction in base pay"). B built the more elegant frame — the workweek is already legislated, the only question is the number; a coordination trap explains non-diffusion; the status quo's costs are real but borne invisibly by workers. But A landed the more damaging and better-weighed attack: gross cost is universal and certain while the productivity offsets are sectoral and drawn from self-selected voluntary pilots, so a universal mandate needs all firms to gain when the evidence shows only some do. A's pressure question on hospital funding forced B into an honest but costly concession ("the public purse pays it"), which A converted into a memorable indictment — a large spending program routed through labour law so it never faces a budget vote — and A's point that agency/retraining costs are a fraction of payroll while the mandate adds a quarter to every covered hour went largely unanswered. A also answered B's sharpest pressure (why not repeal forty?) directly and coherently on incidence, and offered a genuinely useful reframe: universal overtime repricing without the pay-protection clause, "coordination without confiscation," which neutralised the first-mover trap that was B's core reason for statute. B's best counter — that A's scheme makes the worker buy her own day off out of wages, and that "uncosted to the firm is not costless to society" — is a real hit and keeps B competitive, and B's Ford exchange partly blunts A's voluntary-adoption claim. It was not enough to repair the sectoral-asymmetry and funding-incidence hole. A also carried two clipped turns as an execution cost, which trims the margin.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's pressure question demanding who funds a pay-protected hour cut in hospitals, and the follow-up weighing after B answered "the public purse pays it": A reframed the concession as an enormous, unbudgeted spending program smuggled through labour law, and showed the "burnout budget" offsets are far smaller than a 25% payroll increase. B's reply that society has always bought rest deliberately was principled but never met the scale or incidence objection.</best_rebuttal>
